note: A look upward from under lowered brows, with the head bent forward.
Stubborn and determined; refusing to give up.
Dressed. British spelling of “appareled.”
Ports in Asia. Europeans of the time called South and East Asia “the East.”
A ship-chandler sells supplies to ships. His water-clerk boats out to arriving ships to win their business.
Sailors call a ship “she,” so “her captain” means the ship’s captain.
Showing off; a display meant to impress.
In good enough condition to sail safely at sea.
Iron rods with a hook at one end, used on deck to haul and handle the anchor chain.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Chain-hook”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: The cable is the heavy rope or chain that connects a ship to its anchor.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Cable”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Gold-leaf is gold beaten into very thin sheets, sold in small booklets and used to gild carvings.
The stern is the back end of a ship.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Stern”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: A parlour is a sitting room for receiving visitors.
A voyage of three months outward, from a home port to a distant one.
Job, in the Bible’s Book of Job, loses his wealth, children, and health but keeps his faith in God. The Epistle of James speaks of “the patience of Job.”
source: The Bible (King James Version), Job 1–2; James 5:11, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

note: Cheerful fun and good humour.
A close friend who shares in drinking and good times.
Humouring: going along with someone’s wishes or moods to keep them happy.
Fidelity: loyalty. A fiend is a devil or evil spirit.
Quit the job suddenly; give it up.
“Confounded” was a mild curse word, like “damned.”
Exquisite here means intense or keen, not “beautiful.” Sensibility means sensitivity of feeling.
An incognito is a hidden identity, used to avoid being recognized.
A military phrase: an army that retreats “in good order” withdraws without panic, keeping its ranks.
Now Mumbai: the chief seaport of western India, then under British rule. It is the first and westernmost of the ports in this list.
Now Kolkata: a port city in eastern India, on the Hooghly (Hugli) River. Around 1900 it was the capital of British India.
Now Yangon: the capital and chief port of Burma (now Myanmar), then ruled by Britain as part of British India.
An island off the northwest coast of the Malay Peninsula, now part of Malaysia. The British founded a settlement there in 1786; from 1826 it was part of the British colony of the Straits Settlements.
Now Jakarta, on the north coast of Java. The Dutch founded the city in 1619, and it was the capital of all the Dutch settlements in the East. It is the farthest east of the ports listed.
Stopping places on a journey.
Forest that has never been cut or cleared by people.
The Malay people, native to the Malay Peninsula and nearby islands of Southeast Asia.
Elected: chosen, decided of his own will.
A word of one syllable; here, the name “Jim.”
Tuan is a Malay title of respect meaning “master” or “lord,” given to Europeans and to Malays of rank.
source: R. J. Wilkinson, A Malay-English Dictionary (1901), “tuwan”, https://archive.org/details/aeg2034.0001.001.umich.edu

note: A parsonage is the house provided for a parish clergyman (a parson).
Ships that carry cargo or passengers for trade, not warships.
Abodes: homes. Piety: devotion to religion.
Whatever lies beyond human knowledge; here, God and the truths of religion.
Providence: God, thought of as guiding and caring for the world. Unerring: never making a mistake.
The house of a rector, the clergyman in charge of a parish.
Small patches of lawn in a garden.
A church post that comes with a house and income (a benefice), not “a way of earning money.”
Easy, entertaining reading, such as adventure stories, read for fun.
A vocation is a strong feeling of being called to a particular career.
A ship moored in a river and used as a school for boys training to be merchant officers. HMS Conway, an old navy frigate moored in the River Mersey, opened as such a school in 1859.
source: National Museums Liverpool, “Records of HMS Conway, training ship”, https://www.liverpoolmuseums.org.uk/artifact/records-of-hms-conway-training-ship; HMS Conway history site, https://hmsconway.org/history_mersey.html

note: The mercantile marine is the merchant navy: a nation’s trading ships and their crews.
Hoist the top-gallant yards (crossbars for sails, third level above deck) and fix them across the mast.
source: Merriam-Webster, “topgallant”, https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/topgallant; W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “All”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Third best in his class at navigation, the skill of working out a ship’s position and course.
Rowed as stroke oar: the rower nearest the stern, who sets the pace the other rowers follow.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Stroke-oar”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: One of a ship’s boats, rowed with oars and able to carry a sail. “First” is its number.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Cutters of a ship”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Smart: quick and skilful. Aloft: up in the masts and rigging.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Aloft”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: A platform at the head of the lower foremast (the front mast), where sailors work the sails above.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Top”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Straight up and down; vertical.
Wide. A ship’s beam is its width at the widest point.
A deck below the upper decks. On this training ship it is where the boys spend their time below.
From the Tower of Babel in the Bible, where God makes the builders speak different languages so they cannot understand each other. A “babel” is a noisy confusion of voices.
source: The Bible (King James Version), Genesis 11:1–9, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10; Merriam-Webster, “babel”, https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/babel

note: In a severe storm a crew might chop down the masts to save the ship from capsizing.
A line is a rope. Carrying one ashore from a wreck lets others be pulled to safety.
A person left stranded, usually after a shipwreck.
Keep away; hold off for a while.
Quelled: put down. A mutiny is a revolt by sailors against their officers.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Mutiny”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: On a ship, the steep stairs between decks are called ladders.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Ladder”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: An opening in a deck leading to the deck below.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Hatchway”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Confounded here means confused and astonished.
A gale is a very strong wind. When wind freshens, it grows stronger.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Fresh”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Salvoes: several guns fired at the same moment.
Craft: boats and other small vessels.
Pitching: a ship’s front and back rising and falling in turn as it meets the waves. Ponderously: heavily.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Pitching”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Floating platforms where passengers get on and off boats. They rise and fall with the tide.
Jostled: pushed roughly in a crowd.
An order for the boat’s crew to take their places in the cutter.
A ship that trades along a coast, between nearby ports.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Coaster”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Sailing into the river to escape the storm.
A sailing vessel with two or more masts, rigged mainly with fore-and-aft sails (sails set lengthwise along the ship).
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Schooner”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: The rail: the guard along the outer edge of a ship’s deck.
Small cranes sticking out over a ship’s side, used to raise and lower its boats.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Davit”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: On a ship with three masts, the mast nearest the stern (back).
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Mizen-mast”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Moorings are anchors and heavy chains fixed in the riverbed, to which a ship is made fast.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Moorings”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: With her bow (front) pointing into the wind.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Head to wind”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Scanty: small in amount; less than enough.
The ropes that hold up a ship’s masts and work its sails.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Rigging”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: The order to lower the boat into the water.
The falls are the tackle ropes that lower a boat from the davits; once afloat, the crew frees it.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Fall”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Seethed: churned and foamed, like boiling water.
Level with the ship, side by side.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Abreast”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: An order to row together, in time with the stroke oar.
Whelps: puppies. Here, a rough, scolding name for the boys.
The bow is the front end of a boat.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Bow”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Smart here means quick and alert, not clever.
Loose boards laid in the bottom of a rowing boat to stand and sit on.
Contemptible: deserving scorn; not worth being afraid of.
Inefficient here means having no real effect; the danger did no harm.
Affront: face boldly. Perils: dangers.
Sat by himself, thinking gloomily.
The rower nearest the bow, who handles the boat-hook.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Bowman”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: A boat-hook is a pole with a metal hook, used to push off, pull in, or grab things.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Boat-hook”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Breeches: trousers, especially ones that end at the knee.
The tiller is the handle used to turn the rudder and steer the boat.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Tiller”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Swamped: filled with water, almost sinking.
Chap: British slang for a man or fellow.
Awfully: very; used in casual speech.
Fancy: imagine. Used to show surprise.
Caused great excitement among the listening boys.
Ministered to: served or fed.
Spurious: false; not genuine, only seeming real.
Was enough for the purpose.
Flinched: drew back in fear.
Calmly and coolly, without strong feeling.
Exulted: felt great joy and triumph.
Certitude: certainty; a feeling of being sure.
Avidity: eagerness; a strong, hungry desire.
